episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Working Lands & Industry
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Working Lands & Industry.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: Is trust something you build, or something you inherit?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down Lac La Hache Arena to be closed for season and B.C. Conservatives costed platform relies on economic growth that beats all forecasts, plus 11 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: Does a forest-products sector that is shifting toward high-value markets and a 45 million cubic metre harvest target actually serve Cariboo communities, and whose numbers should residents trust while that shift happens? Topics include: Hitachi Energy's pressboard plant and whether B.C. fibre benefits from it, Mass timber market size and how completed, under-construction and planned projects are counted, The 45 million cubic metre harvest target and the gap between allowable cut and actual harvest, Trust in official versus leaked harvest data and the role of independent audit, Retraining outcomes for displaced workers, including the TRU heavy equipment program and placement tracking.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Williams Lake Stampede Association

discussion.central_question: Does a forest-products sector that is shifting toward high-value markets and a 45 million cubic metre harvest target actually serve Cariboo communities, and whose numbers should residents trust while that shift happens?
discussion.riley_position: Value is moving up the supply chain, and permit reform is the fastest lever a province can pull to convert legal but uncut volume into jobs; published, reconciled harvest data would make any target checkable and rebuild trust.
riley_key_evidence: Hitachi Energy's $479 million transformer pressboard plant in London, Ontario, with about $50 million in public money, shows forest fibre becoming a high-tech input.
Environmental Reporting BC data show public-land harvest about 22 per cent below the allowable annual cut over 20 years, meaning legal volume already exists to be cut.
Mass timber is a scaled market, with the Forest Products Association of Canada's Mass Timber Roadmap reporting almost 700 completed buildings.
discussion.casey_position: Demand and harvest targets are being framed by parties with a stake in the numbers; without a buyer, a hiring link, and an audited harvest record, a permit fix will not save mill towns, and retraining is only worth it if graduates are still working a year later.
casey_key_evidence: Hitachi's announcement names no B.C. fibre source, so public money in the plant is spent in London while the Cariboo gets no guaranteed demand.
Mass timber counts differ across sources (the roadmap's pipeline is over 140 projects, the FSC column says over 200), so 'booming' depends on which stage is being counted.
The Thompson Rivers University Heavy Equipment Operator program, built for workers from the West Fraser 100 Mile Lumber closure, has no reported placement tracking after graduation.
discussion.resolution: They did not converge. Riley agreed the hiring link and published reconciliation of allowable cut versus actual harvest are missing and should be added, and Casey agreed the Quesnel council request should carry the reconciliation question. They still disagreed on the bottleneck, with Riley favouring permits and Casey favouring a mill and a buyer, and they agreed the buyer question and the audit question remain unresolved.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE
These analytical threads were identified before generation. Use the findings to ground Riley's and Casey's arguments with real evidence — develop them as substantive exchanges, not a citation list. Cite naturally.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the "mass timber is booming" claim (700+ completed, 200+ in progress) consistent with other sources, and how solid is the underlying data?
Findings: The FSC Canada piece's "more than 700 completed" figure is in line with industry counts. The Forest Products Association of Canada's Mass Timber Roadmap says "almost 700" buildings completed, with more than 140 under construction or in planning, a noticeably smaller pipeline than the 200+ cited in the op-ed. Natural Resources Canada's SMTC-linked interactive map covers over 750 completed or under-construction projects from 2007 to 2022, so the counts depend on the database, dates, and whether "in planning" projects are included. Figures are therefore a snapshot, not a settled total.
Suggested angle: Riley can point to the 40% of projects finished in the last few years as proof of real momentum and scaling. Casey can press that "in progress" and "in planning" are not the same thing, and that pipeline numbers from industry-adjacent groups should be read with care. Ask who counts a project as "booming" and what happens to wood supply if demand arrives faster than sustainable harvest.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What exactly is in the Hitachi Energy London, Ontario investment, and is it a forestry story?
Findings: Hitachi Energy announced a $479-million Transformer Insulation Centre in London, Ontario (Oct. 16, 2026), described as Canada's first electrical-grade pressboard factory. Public money totals about $50 million: $20 million from the federal Strategic Response Fund, $10 million from Natural Resources Canada's Investments in Forest Industry Transformation program, and up to $20 million from Ontario's Invest Ontario Fund. Hitachi is funding the bulk of the project. Pressboard is a wood-fibre material used inside nearly every high-voltage transformer, and the plant is framed around demand from data centres, green energy, and industrial growth.
Suggested angle: This is a good case of forest-industry transformation pulling wood fibre into the electrical grid rather than housing. Riley can argue it shows how forest products are becoming high-tech inputs for the energy transition. Casey can ask how much of the ~$50 million is public versus private leverage, whether the factory's fibre supply is secured locally, and whether a grid-driven boom will bring jobs to forest-dependent towns or just to southern Ontario.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What are the B.C. Conservative forestry promises, and how do they compare with the actual harvest record?
Findings: The B.C. Conservative platform commits to raising the provincial harvest to at least 45 million cubic metres a year, alongside faster permitting, cuts to permitting costs, and expanded forest-sector support. Reporting notes the province cut just under 30 million cubic metres last year, roughly half of the 60 million the sector was historically cut. Environmental Reporting BC data show that over the past 20 years, public-land harvest ran about 22% below the Allowable Annual Cut (average AAC of 77 million m³ vs. average harvest of 60 million m³). The 45 million target is also the one the NDP government previously set (Premier Eby's mandate letter directed the forests minister to "enable harvest of 45 million cubic metres per year, while fulfilling our commitment to protect old growth"). A leaked report cited by the Ancient Forest Alliance and Business in Vancouver argues the harvest is overestimated, and Wood Business describes the path to 45 million as "challenging."
Suggested angle: Both parties share the 45-million goal, so the real dispute is how to get there. Riley can argue that permitting delays and red tape are the bottleneck and that a faster approval system unlocks supply and jobs for mill towns. Casey can counter that the cut has been persistently below the AAC for two decades, which suggests the constraint is markets, labour, and mill capacity, not just permits, and that old-growth commitments and inflated AAC estimates make a higher target a risk to the forests themselves. The Williams Lake/South Cariboo story about displaced workers retraining at TRU is a human test of who benefits from either plan.

(Ballot researched Thursday October 15 and unchanged since. Background, not news.)
ELECTION RESEARCH — 2026 B.C. provincial general election

Background for the roundup's election stories and any race the hosts mention. It is not the deep dive's subject.

**FINDINGS — Cariboo-Chilcotin**

Filed candidates: Kathryn Askew (BC NDP), Lorne Doerkson (Conservative), Douglas Gook (BC Green). Elections BC's candidate report lists all three (elections.bc.ca, candidate website report, Oct. 2026), and BC Ballot and Studio X News carry the same names.

- **Kathryn Askew (BC NDP).** 100 Mile Free Press (Oct. 1, 2026) reports she is a retired school teacher from Canim Lake, named as the NDP candidate. The BC NDP release names her as its Cariboo-Chilcotin candidate (bcndp.ca, undated in my read) and says she has 32 years in education, including leadership roles with the BC Teachers' Federation and her local union. The release also says that in 2025 she was the NDP candidate for Mission—Matsqui—Abbotsford in the federal election. I did not find her vote share in that race. Stephen Taylor's 2025 results page reports Brad Vis (Conservative) won that riding with 56.7% and Jeff Howe (Liberal) placed second with 36.6% (stephentaylor.ca, 2025 results). No controversy involving Askew was found in the sources read.

- **Lorne Doerkson (Conservative).** Sourced background: MLA for Cariboo-Chilcotin since 2020, first elected as a B.C. Liberal, re-elected in 2024 as a B.C. Conservative (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). BC Ballot gives the 2024 Conservative margin in the riding as 7,722 votes (bcballot.ca, 2026 candidate page). Carried forward from prior research: Elections BC's 2020 statement of votes shows him at 6,600 votes (51.25%) for the Liberals. The Globe and Mail (Sept. 26, 2026) reports he took over as Conservative leader. Wikipedia describes him as interim leader since 2026.
  - *Controversy (campaign, 2026):* Vaughn Palmer's Vancouver Sun column (Oct. 7, 2026) says Doerkson told reporters he had made "no promises at all" on auto insurance, and Palmer argues he had made four. Palmer writes that Doerkson twice denied making commitments of any kind. This is the columnist's assessment, and the outlet's article was paywalled in my read. Doerkson's response is the denial reported in that column.
  - *Related party matter (not about Doerkson personally):* The Tyee (Oct. 8, 2026) reports Doerkson fired the party's Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate after social media posts the BC NDP flagged as racist. CityNews (Oct. 14, 2026) reports a Conservative campaign director under fire over social posts will stay on, Doerkson says.
  - No other controversy involving Doerkson was established in the sources checked.

- **Douglas Gook (BC Green).** Elections BC's candidate report lists him for Cariboo-Chilcotin (2026). The Caledonia Courier (Oct. 2024) reports he had run unsuccessfully as a Green candidate in North Cariboo, now Prince George-Cariboo North, four times, including a 2017 Nechako Lakes bid where he took about nine per cent. My Cariboo Now calls his 2020 bid his fourth time running for the Greens in that riding. Carried forward from prior research: the Elections BC 2020 statement of votes shows him at 707 votes (6.38%) in Cariboo North. The two accounts don't reconcile the count of runs, and the show has not resolved it. CKPG Today (Sept. 13, 2024) announced him as the Green candidate for Nechako Lakes in 2024. His 2024 result in that riding was not established in the sources read. No controversy was established.

**FINDINGS — Prince George-North Cariboo (includes Quesnel)**

Filed candidates: Denice Bardua (BC NDP), Sheldon Clare (Conservative), Randy Thompson (BC Green). The Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports the list was confirmed by Elections BC after nominations closed Oct. 3. CKPG Today (Oct. 3, 2026) and the Prince George Citizen (candidates finalized) list the same three.

- **Denice Bardua (BC NDP).** CKPG Today (Sept. 24, 2024) reports she was announced as the NDP candidate for this riding in 2024. Her campaign site (denicebardua.bcndp.ca) says she has been a Quesnel resident since 1997 and works in education. BCPoliTracker reports she placed second in 2024 with 3,426 votes, or 17.0%, behind the Conservative candidate. Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) gives 17.03% for 2024. Her 2024 run is the only earlier run established in the sources read. No controversy was established.

- **Sheldon Clare (Conservative, incumbent).** Sourced background: won the riding for the B.C. Conservatives in 2024 (Elections BC results, 2024-10-19). Carried forward from prior research: Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports 11,430 votes, or 56.82%, in 2024. Times Colonist (Jan. 8, 2026, Canadian Press) reports he said he was running for the B.C. Conservative leadership. CFJC Today (Feb. 28, 2026) reports he suspended that bid, citing a leadership application issue where some signatures were not accepted. He said he "takes full responsibility."
  - *Election-finance penalty (finding):* Elections BC's enforcement notice (dated March 30, 2026) and its April 1, 2026 release (reported by CKPG Today, Apr. 1, 2026, and the Quesnel Cariboo Observer, Apr. 3, 2026) say he was fined $1,500 for accepting anonymous contributions for the 2024 election that exceeded the limit by about $4,000. Elections BC said the investigation found no deliberate attempt to circumvent the law. The Prince George Citizen reported the same penalty. I did not find his response to the penalty in the sources read.
  - *Allegation (Sept. 2026):* CKPG Today (Sept. 18, 2026) reports that in a party group chat about municipal elections, Clare wrote "There's a good number that need hanging," responding to a post by a Parksville mayoral candidate. Clare's statement says the remark was made in jest, was not meant as a threat, and he apologized to anyone who took offense (CKPG Today, Sept. 18, 2026; Prince George Citizen update). The Prince George Citizen headlined his apology as a formal apology. The BC NDP wrote on X that Doerkson "had one last chance to drop him. He didn't." That is the NDP's claim, and Doerkson's response to it was not found.
  - *Allegation (undated in snippet):* PressProgress reports residential-school postings attributed to Clare. The article says neither Clare nor the party responded to its requests for comment. The article's date and full text were not confirmed in my read, and the content appears to predate the 2026 campaign.

- **Randy Thompson (BC Green).** BC Greens' candidate page says he ran as the Green candidate in this riding in 2024 and previously served two years on the party's provincial council (bcgreens.ca). Quesnel Cariboo Observer (Oct. 7, 2026) reports he finished fourth in 2024 with just over four per cent. BCPoliTracker gives 866 votes, 4.3%. Prince George Daily News (Oct. 11, 2026) reports the Greens announced him as the candidate. No controversy was established.

The show has not yet established any earlier provincial election run for Kathryn Askew, Denice Bardua or Randy Thompson.
